claim: Class IV ddaC neurons specifically prune larval dendrites without affecting axons during Drosophila metamorphosis.
source: Class IV ddaC neurons specifically prune larval dendrites without affecting axons during Drosophila metamorphosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of ddaC neurons.

claim: ddaC neurons distribute the minus ends of microtubules to dendrites but the plus ends to axons.
source: ddaCs distribute the minus ends of microtubules (MTs) to dendrites but the plus ends to axons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of ddaC neurons.

claim: Patronin is a minus-end-binding protein crucial for ddaC dendrite pruning.
source: Here, we identified Patronin, a minus-end-binding protein, for its crucial and dose-sensitive role in ddaC dendrite pruning.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The CKK domain is important for Patronin's function in dendrite pruning.
source: The CKK domain is important for Patronin's function in dendrite pruning.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by rescue experiments with domain deletion constructs shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both patronin knockdown and overexpression resulted in a drastic decrease of MT minus ends in ddaC dendrites.
source: Moreover, we show that both patronin knockdown and overexpression resulted in a drastic decrease of MT minus ends and a concomitant increase of plus-end-out MTs in ddaC dendrites, suggesting that Patronin stabilizes dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Nod-β-gal distribution data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both patronin knockdown and overexpression resulted in a concomitant increase of plus-end-out MTs in ddaC dendrites.
source: Moreover, we show that both patronin knockdown and overexpression resulted in a drastic decrease of MT minus ends and a concomitant increase of plus-end-out MTs in ddaC dendrites, suggesting that Patronin stabilizes dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by EB1-GFP comet tracking data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Patronin stabilizes dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
source: Moreover, we show that both patronin knockdown and overexpression resulted in a drastic decrease of MT minus ends and a concomitant increase of plus-end-out MTs in ddaC dendrites, suggesting that Patronin stabilizes dendritic minus-end-out MTs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the MT orientation data.

claim: Attenuation of Klp10A MT depolymerase in patronin mutant neurons significantly restored minus-end-out MTs in dendrites.
source: Consistently, attenuation of Klp10A MT depolymerase in patronin mutant neurons significantly restored minus-end-out MTs in dendrites and thereby rescued dendrite-pruning defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by double RNAi experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Attenuation of Klp10A MT depolymerase in patronin mutant neurons rescued dendrite-pruning defects.
source: Consistently, attenuation of Klp10A MT depolymerase in patronin mutant neurons significantly restored minus-end-out MTs in dendrites and thereby rescued dendrite-pruning defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by double RNAi experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Patronin orients minus-end-out MT arrays in dendrites to promote dendrite-specific pruning mainly through antagonizing Klp10A activity.
source: Thus, our study demonstrates that Patronin orients minus-end-out MT arrays in dendrites to promote dendrite-specific pruning mainly through antagonizing Klp10A activity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pruning is a developmental process referred to as selective removal of unwanted neurites without causing neuronal death.
source: Pruning is a developmental process referred to as selective removal of unwanted neurites, for example axons, dendrites, or synapses, without causing neuronal death.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the introduction based on established knowledge.

claim: Defects in neuronal pruning result in larger dendritic spine density in layer V pyramidal neurons of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) patients.
source: Defects in neuronal pruning result in larger dendritic spine density in layer V pyramidal neurons of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) patients (Tang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Tang et al., 2014.

claim: MB γ neurons prune their dorsal and medial axon branches as well as entire dendrites during metamorphosis.
source: In the central nervous system (CNS), mushroom body (MB) γ neurons prune their dorsal and medial axon branches as well as entire dendrites, and subsequently re-extend the medial branches to be part of the adult-specific circuits (Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Lee et al., 1999.

claim: Class I da (ddaD/ddaE) and class IV da (C4da or ddaC) neurons prune away all their larval dendrites but leave their axons intact.
source: In the peripheral nervous system (PNS), some dendritic arborization (da) neurons, including class I da (ddaD/ddaE) and class IV da (C4da or ddaC) neurons, prune away all their larval dendrites but leave their axons intact (Williams and Truman, 2005; Kuo et al., 2005)
evidence: This is cited from Williams and Truman, 2005 and Kuo et al., 2005.

claim: Class III da neurons (ddaA/ddaF) are eliminated via apoptosis during the first day of metamorphosis.
source: whereas class III da neurons (ddaA/ddaF) are eliminated via apoptosis during the first day of metamorphosis (Williams and Truman, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Williams and Truman, 2005.

claim: ddaC dendrites are initially severed at their proximal regions as early as 4 hr after puparium formation (APF).
source: Upon induction of the steroid hormone 20-hydroxyecdysone (ecdysone) at late larval stage, ddaC dendrites are initially severed at their proximal regions as early as 4 hr after puparium formation (APF), followed by rapid fragmentation and debris clearance (Figure 1A) (Williams and Truman, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Williams and Truman, 2005 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Ecdysone binds to a heterodimeric receptor complex consisting of the Ecdysone receptor and its co-receptor Ultraspiracle.
source: Ecdysone binds to a heterodimeric receptor complex, which consists of the Ecdysone receptor and its co-receptor Ultraspiracle, to induce several downstream effectors, including a key transcription factor Sox14 (Kirilly et al., 2009; Kirilly et al., 2011), a cytoskeletal regulator Mical (Kirilly et al., 2009), Headcase (Loncle and Williams, 2012), a Cullin1 E3 ligase complex (Wong et al., 2013), and calcium signaling (Kanamori et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: Cytoskeletal disassembly, especially microtubule (MT) disassembly, is a key step of pruning occurring before the detachment of neurites in both MB γ and ddaC neurons.
source: Cytoskeletal disassembly, especially microtubule (MT) disassembly, is a key step of pruning occurring before the detachment of neurites in both MB γ and ddaC neurons (Watts et al., 2003; Williams and Truman, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Watts et al., 2003 and Williams and Truman, 2005.

claim: Katanin p60-like 1 (Kat-60L1) is required for dendrite pruning of ddaC neurons.
source: Katanin p60-like 1 (Kat-60L1), a putative MT severing factor, is required for dendrite pruning of ddaC neurons (Lee et al., 2009)
evidence: This is cited from Lee et al., 2009.

claim: Katanin 60 (Kat-60), Spastin and Fidgetin appear to be dispensable for dendrite pruning of ddaC neurons.
source: whereas other MT severing factors, including Katanin 60 (Kat-60), Spastin and Fidgetin, appear to be dispensable (Lee et al., 2009; Stone et al., 2014; Tao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Lee et al., 2009; Stone et al., 2014; Tao et al., 2016.

claim: Mammalian Spastin mediates branch-specific disassembly of MTs and facilitates synapse elimination in the developing mouse neuromuscular junctions.
source: In contrast, mammalian Spastin mediates branch-specific disassembly of MTs and facilitates synapse elimination in the developing mouse neuromuscular junctions (Brill et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Brill et al., 2016.

claim: Par-1 is required for increased MT dynamics and dendrite pruning in ddaC neurons.
source: A recent study indicated that Par-1, whose mammalian ortholog is a Tau kinase, is required for increased MT dynamics and dendrite pruning in ddaC neurons. Par-1 promotes MT breakdown mainly via Tau inhibition (Herzmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Herzmann et al., 2017.

claim: Par-1 promotes MT breakdown mainly via Tau inhibition.
source: A recent study indicated that Par-1, whose mammalian ortholog is a Tau kinase, is required for increased MT dynamics and dendrite pruning in ddaC neurons. Par-1 promotes MT breakdown mainly via Tau inhibition (Herzmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Herzmann et al., 2017.

claim: Axonal MTs are mainly aligned in a plus-end-out pattern in differentiated mammalian neurons.
source: In differentiated mammalian neurons, axons and dendrites differ in MT orientation: axonal MTs are mainly aligned in a plus-end-out pattern, whereas MTs are mixed at the proximal dendritic region with both minus-end-out and plus-end-out arrays (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015.

claim: MTs are mixed at the proximal dendritic region with both minus-end-out and plus-end-out arrays in differentiated mammalian neurons.
source: In differentiated mammalian neurons, axons and dendrites differ in MT orientation: axonal MTs are mainly aligned in a plus-end-out pattern, whereas MTs are mixed at the proximal dendritic region with both minus-end-out and plus-end-out arrays (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015.

claim: In Drosophila and C. elegans neurons, axons contain nearly uniform plus-end-out MTs.
source: In Drosophila and C. elegans neurons, axons, like mammalian ones, contain nearly uniform plus-end-out MTs, however, MTs are oriented almost exclusively minus-end-out in major dendrites but mainly plus-end-out in shorter terminal dendrites (Stone et al., 2008; Rolls et al., 2007; Ori-McKenney et al., 2012; Goodwin et al., 2012; Yalgin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: MTs are oriented almost exclusively minus-end-out in major dendrites of Drosophila and C. elegans neurons.
source: In Drosophila and C. elegans neurons, axons, like mammalian ones, contain nearly uniform plus-end-out MTs, however, MTs are oriented almost exclusively minus-end-out in major dendrites but mainly plus-end-out in shorter terminal dendrites (Stone et al., 2008; Rolls et al., 2007; Ori-McKenney et al., 2012; Goodwin et al., 2012; Yalgin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: MTs are mainly plus-end-out in shorter terminal dendrites of Drosophila and C. elegans neurons.
source: In Drosophila and C. elegans neurons, axons, like mammalian ones, contain nearly uniform plus-end-out MTs, however, MTs are oriented almost exclusively minus-end-out in major dendrites but mainly plus-end-out in shorter terminal dendrites (Stone et al., 2008; Rolls et al., 2007; Ori-McKenney et al., 2012; Goodwin et al., 2012; Yalgin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: In C. elegans, kinesin-1 was proposed to regulate predominant minus-end-out orientation of dendritic MTs through gliding plus-end-out MTs out of the dendrites.
source: In C. elegans, kinesin-1 was proposed to regulate predominant minus-end-out orientation of dendritic MTs through gliding plus-end-out MTs out of the dendrites (Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Yan et al., 2013.

claim: In Drosophila, minus-end-out orientation of dendritic MTs depends on +TIPs, plus-end-directed motor protein kinesin-1/2 as well as MT regulators γ-Tubulin/Centrosomin.
source: In Drosophila, minus-end-out orientation of dendritic MTs depends on +TIPs, plus-end-directed motor protein kinesin-1/2 as well as MT regulators γ-Tubulin/Centrosomin (Mattie et al., 2010; Ori-McKenney et al., 2012; Nguyen et al., 2014; Herzmann et al., 2018; Yalgin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: The Patronin family of proteins have been identified as conserved MT minus-end-binding proteins.
source: The Patronin family of proteins have been identified as conserved MT minus-end-binding proteins, which contain Patronin in Drosophila, calmodulin-regulated spectrin-associated protein 1/2/3 (CAMSAP1/2/3) in mammals, and PTRN-1 in worms (Baines et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Baines et al., 2009.

claim: Patronin/CAMSAP/PTRN-1 contains a calponin homology (CH) domain at its amino-terminus, three predicted coiled-coil (CC) domains at its central region, and a CAMSAP/KIAA1078/KIA1543 (CKK) domain at its carboxyl-terminus.
source: Patronin/CAMSAP/PTRN-1 contains a calponin homology (CH) domain at its amino-terminus, three predicted coiled-coil (CC) domains at its central region, and a CAMSAP/KIAA1078/KIA1543 (CKK) domain at its carboxyl-terminus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Baines et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Baines et al., 2009 and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: patronin (also known as ssp4) was first identified to regulate the length of mitotic spindle in Drosophila S2 cells.
source: patronin (also known as ssp4) was first identified to regulate the length of mitotic spindle in Drosophila S2 cells (Goshima et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Goshima et al., 2007.

claim: The Patronin proteins recognize and stabilize free minus ends by protecting them from kinesin-13-mediated depolymerization.
source: The Patronin proteins recognize and stabilize free minus ends by protecting them from kinesin-13-mediated depolymerization (Goodwin and Vale, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Goodwin and Vale, 2010.

claim: Mammalian CAMSAP3/Nezha anchors MT minus ends to adherence junctions and controls the apical-basal MT orientation in cultured epithelial cells.
source: Mammalian CAMSAP3/Nezha anchors MT minus ends to adherence junctions and controls the apical-basal MT orientation in cultured epithelial cells (Meng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Meng et al., 2008.

claim: Both Patronin and CAMSAP3 can polarize MT arrays via actin-crosslinking proteins.
source: Both Patronin and CAMSAP3 can polarize MT arrays via actin-crosslinking proteins (Ning et al., 2016; Nashchekin et al., 2016; Khanal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: In hippocampal neurons, CAMSAP2 localizes to the MT minus ends and plays an important role in axon specification and dendrite formation.
source: In hippocampal neurons, CAMSAP2 localizes to the MT minus ends and plays an important role in axon specification and dendrite formation (Yau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Yau et al., 2014.

claim: In C. elegans neurons, PTRN-1 is required for synaptic vesicle localization, neurite morphology and axon regeneration.
source: In C. elegans neurons, PTRN-1 is required for synaptic vesicle localization, neurite morphology and axon regeneration (Chuang et al., 2014; Marcette et al., 2014; Richardson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claim: Wild-type ddaC neurons pruned all their dendrites at 16 hr APF.
source: While the wild-type neurons pruned all the dendrites (B), ddaC neurons overexpressing patronin RNAi #1 (C), patroninc9-c5 (D) or patronink07433 (F) MARCM ddaC clones exhibited simple arbors at WP stage and dendrite pruning defects at 16 hr APF.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and quantified in Figure 1G and H.

claim: ddaC neurons overexpressing patronin RNAi #1 exhibited dendrite pruning defects at 16 hr APF.
source: While the wild-type neurons pruned all the dendrites (B), ddaC neurons overexpressing patronin RNAi #1 (C), patroninc9-c5 (D) or patronink07433 (F) MARCM ddaC clones exhibited simple arbors at WP stage and dendrite pruning defects at 16 hr APF.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and quantified in Figure 1G and H.

claim: patroninc9-c5 MARCM ddaC clones exhibited dendrite pruning defects at 16 hr APF.
source: While the wild-type neurons pruned all the dendrites (B), ddaC neurons overexpressing patronin RNAi #1 (C), patroninc9-c5 (D) or patronink07433 (F) MARCM ddaC clones exhibited simple arbors at WP stage and dendrite pruning defects at 16 hr APF.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and quantified in Figure 1G and H.

claim: patronink07433 MARCM ddaC clones exhibited dendrite pruning defects at 16 hr APF.
source: While the wild-type neurons pruned all the dendrites (B), ddaC neurons overexpressing patronin RNAi #1 (C), patroninc9-c5 (D) or patronink07433 (F) MARCM ddaC clones exhibited simple arbors at WP stage and dendrite pruning defects at 16 hr APF.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and quantified in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Low-level expression of mCherry-Patronin fully restored the elaborate arbors at WP and rescued the pruning defects at 16 hr APF in patroninc9-c5 MARCM ddaC clones.
source: Low-level expression of mCherry-Patronin under the control of the UASp promoter fully restored the elaborate arbors at WP and rescued the pruning defects at 16 hr APF in patroninc9-c5 MARCM ddaC clones (E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and quantified in Figure 1G and H.

claim: On average, 606 µm of larval dendrites in patronin RNAi ddaC neurons remained attached to their mutant somas at 16 hr APF.
source: On average, 606 µm and 701 µm of larval dendrites in patronin RNAi and patroninc9-c5 ddaC neurons remained attached to their mutant somas, respectively (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1G.

claim: On average, 701 µm of larval dendrites in patroninc9-c5 ddaC neurons remained attached to their mutant somas at 16 hr APF.
source: On average, 606 µm and 701 µm of larval dendrites in patronin RNAi and patroninc9-c5 ddaC neurons remained attached to their mutant somas, respectively (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1G.

claim: The dendrites of patronin RNAi ddaC neurons were largely removed by 32 hr APF.
source: The dendrites of patronin RNAi ddaC neurons were largely removed by 32 hr APF (n = 32; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), presumably due to extensive apoptosis/migration of the dorsal abdominal epidermis, on which neurons arborize their larval dendrites (Williams and Truman, 2005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and cited from Williams and Truman, 2005.

claim: The dendritic complexity of patroninc9-c5 ddaC clones was greatly compromised at the wandering 3rd instar larval stage (wL3).
source: The dendritic complexity of patroninc9-c5 ddaC clones was greatly compromised at the wandering 3rd instar larval stage (wL3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: patronin RNAi-expressing ddaD/ddaE neurons failed to eliminate their dendrites at 20 hr APF.
source: patronin RNAi-expressing ddaD/ddaE neurons failed to eliminate their dendrites (n = 20, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), similar to patronin ddaC neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: patronin RNAi-expressing ddaF neurons were still apoptotic, similar to wild-type neurons.
source: However, patronin RNAi-expressing ddaF neurons were still apoptotic (n = 14), similar to wild-type neurons (n = 15, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that Patronin is dispensable for neuronal apoptosis during early metamorphosis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Patronin is dispensable for neuronal apoptosis during early metamorphosis.
source: However, patronin RNAi-expressing ddaF neurons were still apoptotic (n = 14), similar to wild-type neurons (n = 15, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that Patronin is dispensable for neuronal apoptosis during early metamorphosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that patronin RNAi does not affect ddaF neuron apoptosis.

claim: Overexpressing either patronin or GFP-patronin transgenes resulted in consistent dendrite pruning defects at 16 hr APF.
source: Importantly, overexpressing either of patronin transgenes, via Gal44-77 (weak driver) or ppk-Gal4 (stronger driver), resulted in consistent dendrite pruning defects at 16 hr APF (Figure 2B and C), which phenocopied patronin mutants (Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and C and quantified in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Overexpression of Patronin via Gal44-77 led to dendrite severing defects in 70% of ddaC neurons with an average of 511 µm dendrites at 16 hr APF.
source: Overexpression of Patronin, via Gal44-77, led to dendrite severing defects in 70% of ddaC neurons with an average of 511 µm dendrites (n = 34; Figure 2B, F and G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and quantified in Figure 2F and G.

claim: When GFP-Patronin was overexpressed at a higher level by two copies of ppk-Gal4, vast majority of ddaC neurons exhibited stronger dendrite severing defects with the persistence of 884 µm dendrites.
source: When GFP-Patronin was overexpressed at a higher level by two copies of ppk-Gal4, vast majority of ddaC neurons exhibited stronger dendrite severing defects with the persistence of 884 µm dendrites (87%, n = 15; Figure 2C, F and G), suggesting that overexpressed Patronin behaves as a dominant negative in dendrite pruning.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Overexpressed Patronin behaves as a dominant negative in dendrite pruning.
source: When GFP-Patronin was overexpressed at a higher level by two copies of ppk-Gal4, vast majority of ddaC neurons exhibited stronger dendrite severing defects with the persistence of 884 µm dendrites (87%, n = 15; Figure 2C, F and G), suggesting that overexpressed Patronin behaves as a dominant negative in dendrite pruning.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-dependent effect of Patronin overexpression on dendrite pruning.

claim: Late-larval induction of GFP-Patronin expression did not affect initial dendrite arborization at WP stage.
source: Late-larval induction of GFP-Patronin expression did not affect initial dendrite arborization at WP stage (n = 8; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E using the Gene-Switch system.

claim: Dendrite severing defects were observed at 16 hr APF in 75% of GFP-Patronin-overexpressing ddaC neurons derived from RU486-fed animals.
source: Notably, dendrite severing defects were observed at 16 hr APF in 75% of GFP-Patronin-overexpressing ddaC neurons derived from RU486-fed animals (n = 16; Figure 2E, F and G), in contrast to no severing defect in non-fed animals (n = 16; Figure 2D, F and G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E and quantified in Figure 2F and G.

claim: The expression of CH-deleted Patronin variant (PatroninΔCH) was able to almost fully rescue the pruning defects in patroninc9-c5 ddaC neurons at 16 hr APF.
source: Notably, the expression of CH-deleted Patronin variant (PatroninΔCH) was able to almost fully rescue the pruning defects in patroninc9-c5 ddaC neurons at 16 hr APF (n = 11; Figure 3B, E and F), similar to the full-length protein (Figure 1E, G and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and quantified in Figure 3E and F.

claim: CKK-deleted Patronin variant (PatroninΔCKK) failed to rescue the dendrite pruning defects in patroninc9-c5 ddaC neurons.
source: However, CKK-deleted Patronin variant (PatroninΔCKK) failed to rescue the dendrite pruning defects in patroninc9-c5 ddaC neurons (n = 10; Figure 3C, E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and quantified in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The expression of the CKK domain significantly rescued patroninc9-c5-associated dendrite pruning defects.
source: Interestingly, the expression of the CKK domain significantly rescued patroninc9-c5-associated dendrite pruning defects (n = 16; Figure 3D, E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and quantified in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Overexpression of PatroninΔCH variant led to prominent dendrite severing defects in ddaC neurons at 16 hr APF.
source: Overexpression of PatroninΔCH variant led to prominent dendrite severing defects in ddaC neurons at 16 hr APF (59%, n = 27, Figure 3H, K and L), similar to the full-length Patronin (69%, n = 16; Figure 3G, K and L).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H and quantified in Figure 3K and L.

claim: The expression of PatroninΔCKK variant did not affect normal dendrite pruning at 16 hr APF.
source: In contrast, the expression of PatroninΔCKK variant did not affect normal dendrite pruning at 16 hr APF (n = 16; Figure 3I, K and L), suggesting that the CKK domain of Patronin is important for its gain-of-function effect on dendrite pruning.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3I and quantified in Figure 3K and L.

claim: The CKK domain of Patronin is important for its gain-of-function effect on dendrite pruning.
source: In contrast, the expression of PatroninΔCKK variant did not affect normal dendrite pruning at 16 hr APF (n = 16; Figure 3I, K and L), suggesting that the CKK domain of Patronin is important for its gain-of-function effect on dendrite pruning.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PatroninΔCKK overexpression does not cause pruning defects.

claim: Overexpression of CKK domain had no effect on dendrite pruning of ddaC neurons.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of CKK domain (n = 16; Figure 3J, K and L), CH domain (n = 25; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or CC1-3 domains (n = 17; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) had no effect on dendrite pruning of ddaC neurons, suggesting that endogenous Patronin protein may function properly to regulate dendrite pruning even with ectopic expression of these individual domains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3J and quantified in Figure 3K and L.

claim: Nod-β-gal was predominantly enriched in dendrites but not in axons in wild-type ddaC neurons.
source: In wild-type ddaC neurons, Nod-β-gal was predominantly enriched in dendrites but not in axons (n = 6, Figure 4A, D and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and quantified in Figure 4D and E.

claim: In all patronin RNAi ddaC neurons, Nod-β-gal was no longer enriched in the dendritic arbors and instead highly concentrated in the soma.
source: Remarkably, in all patronin RNAi ddaC neurons, Nod-β-gal was no longer enriched in the dendritic arbors and instead highly concentrated in the soma (100%, n = 25, Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and quantified in Figure 4D.

claim: All patroninc9-c5 ddaC clones exhibited robust accumulation of Nod-β-gal in the soma concomitantly with its reduced levels in the distal dendrites.
source: Likewise, all patroninc9-c5 ddaC clones also exhibited robust accumulation of Nod-β-gal in the soma concomitantly with its reduced levels in the distal dendrites (100%, n = 11; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4D and E,).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and quantified in Figure 4D and E.

claim: In the dendrites of patronin RNAi or patroninc9-c5 neurons, Nod-β-gal levels were drastically reduced to 12% and 11% of those in the control neurons, respectively.
source: In the dendrites of patronin RNAi or patroninc9-c5 neurons, Nod-β-gal levels were drastically reduced to 12% and 11% of those in the control neurons, respectively (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 4E.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-Patronin resulted in robust accumulation of Nod-β-gal signals in the soma and reduced dendritic distribution in 67% of ddaC neurons.
source: Strikingly, overexpression of GFP-Patronin also resulted in robust accumulation of Nod-β-gal signals in the soma and reduced dendritic distribution in 67% of ddaC neurons (n = 18, Figure 4C, D and E), resembling the patronin mutant phenotypes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and quantified in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Kin-β-gal was localized exclusively to the axons, but not to the dendrites in wild-type ddaC neurons.
source: Kin-β-gal was localized exclusively to the axons, but not to the dendrites in wild-type ddaC neurons (n = 9; Figure 4F and I) (Zheng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F and quantified in Figure 4I, and cited from Zheng et al., 2008.

claim: Kin-β-gal often mis-localized to the dendrites as punctate structures in patronin RNAi ddaC neurons.
source: Interestingly, Kin-β-gal often mis-localized to the dendrites as punctate structures in patronin RNAi (89%, n = 19, Figure 4G and I) or GFP-Patronin-overexpressing ddaC neurons (45%, n = 20, Figure 4H and I), implying an increase of plus-end-out MTs in the dendrites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G and quantified in Figure 4I.

claim: Kin-β-gal often mis-localized to the dendrites as punctate structures in GFP-Patronin-overexpressing ddaC neurons.
source: Interestingly, Kin-β-gal often mis-localized to the dendrites as punctate structures in patronin RNAi (89%, n = 19, Figure 4G and I) or GFP-Patronin-overexpressing ddaC neurons (45%, n = 20, Figure 4H and I), implying an increase of plus-end-out MTs in the dendrites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4H and quantified in Figure 4I.

claim: Patronin localized uniformly to dendrites, axons and soma at larval and WP stages.
source: Patronin localized uniformly to dendrites, axons and soma at larval and WP stages (n = 14 and 14, respectively, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the proximal dendrites, 99% of EB1-GFP comets moved predominantly toward the soma (retrograde) in the control RNAi-expressing ddaC neurons.
source: In the proximal dendrites, 99% of EB1-GFP comets moved predominantly toward the soma (retrograde) in the control RNAi-expressing ddaC neurons (n = 30, Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: In the control ddaC axons, EB1-GFP comets primarily moved away from the soma (anterograde, 96%).
source: In contrast, in the control ddaC axons, EB1-GFP comets primarily moved away from the soma (anterograde, 96%, n = 12, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a plus-end-out MT orientation in axons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The percentage of anterograde EB1-GFP comets was increased to 48% in patronin RNAi #1 ddaC neurons.
source: On average, the percentage of anterograde EB1-GFP comets was increased to 48% and 19% in these patronin RNAi ddaC neurons, respectively (#1, n = 29 neurons, Figure 5B–C; #2, n = 12, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), compared to that in the control neurons (n = 30; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and quantified in Figure 5C.

claim: The percentage of anterograde EB1-GFP comets was increased to 19% in patronin RNAi #2 ddaC neurons.
source: On average, the percentage of anterograde EB1-GFP comets was increased to 48% and 19% in these patronin RNAi ddaC neurons, respectively (#1, n = 29 neurons, Figure 5B–C; #2, n = 12, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), compared to that in the control neurons (n = 30; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The direction of EB1-GFP comets was drastically reversed in 33% of dendrite branches of patronin RNAi #1 ddaC neurons.
source: Notably, the direction of EB1-GFP comets was drastically reversed in 33% of dendrite branches of patronin RNAi #1 ddaC neurons, respectively (n = 43 branches; Figure 5M).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5M.

claim: In 33% of dendrite branches of patronin RNAi #1 ddaC neurons, over 80% of EB1-GFP comets moved away from the soma, suggesting a predominant plus-end-out MT pattern.
source: In these mutant dendrite branches, over 80% of EB1-GFP comets moved away from the soma, suggesting a predominant plus-end-out MT pattern (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5M and interpreted as a plus-end-out MT pattern.

claim: The average numbers of EB1-GFP comets in patronin RNAi #1 expressing ddaC dendrites were not statistically different from that in the control.
source: The average numbers of EB1-GFP comets in patronin RNAi #1 expressing ddaC dendrites were not statistically different from that in the control (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5D.

claim: patronin RNAi knockdown (#1) led to normal EB1-GFP track length.
source: patronin RNAi knockdown (#1) also led to normal EB1-GFP track length (Figure 5E) but slightly higher growth speed (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5E.

claim: patronin RNAi knockdown (#1) led to slightly higher EB1-GFP growth speed.
source: patronin RNAi knockdown (#1) also led to normal EB1-GFP track length (Figure 5E) but slightly higher growth speed (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5F.

claim: The intensity of overall MT levels was significantly reduced in the dendrites of patronin RNAi ddaC neurons.
source: The intensity of overall MT levels was significantly reduced in the dendrites of patronin RNAi ddaC neurons (#1, n = 16), compared with the controls (n = 16; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), as assessed by the antibody 22C10 against Futsch.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: patronin knockdown led to 41% of retrograde EB1-GFP comets in the axons.
source: Compared with 4% of retrograde EB1-GFP comets (predominantly plus-end-out) in the axons of wild-type neurons (n = 12), patronin knockdown led to 41% of retrograde EB1-GFP comets in the axons (n = 17; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicative of a severe defect in the plus-end-out orientation of their axonal MTs upon patronin knockdown.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Patronin overexpression led to a significant increase in anterograde EB1-GFP comets in the ddaC dendrites (10%).
source: Similar to patronin RNAi neurons, Patronin overexpression also led to a significant increase in anterograde EB1-GFP comets in the ddaC dendrites (10%, n = 15; Figure 5H and I), compared to the control neurons (0%, n = 12; Figure 5G and I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H and quantified in Figure 5I.

claim: Patronin overexpression led to an increase in the number of EB1-GFP comets.
source: Patronin overexpression also led to an increase in the number of EB1-GFP comets (Figure 5J) but did not affect normal EB1-GFP track length (Figure 5K) and growth speed (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5J.

claim: Patronin overexpression did not affect normal EB1-GFP track length.
source: Patronin overexpression also led to an increase in the number of EB1-GFP comets (Figure 5J) but did not affect normal EB1-GFP track length (Figure 5K) and growth speed (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5K.

claim: Patronin overexpression did not affect normal EB1-GFP growth speed.
source: Patronin overexpression also led to an increase in the number of EB1-GFP comets (Figure 5J) but did not affect normal EB1-GFP track length (Figure 5K) and growth speed (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5L.

claim: Double knockdown of patronin and klp10A completely restored the retrograde movement of EB1-GFP comets.
source: Double knockdown of patronin and klp10A (patronin +klp10A) completely restored the retrograde movement of EB1-GFP comets (n = 11; Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and quantified in Figure 6C.

claim: All dendrite branches exhibited a uniform minus-end-out MT pattern in patronin +klp10A RNAi neurons.
source: Moreover, all dendrite branches exhibited a uniform minus-end-out MT pattern in patronin +klp10A RNAi neurons (n = 27 branches; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), identical to the control neurons (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Further knockdown of klp10A resulted in no alteration in the number, track length and movement speed of EB1-GFP comets in patronin RNAi dendrites.
source: Moreover, further knockdown of klp10A resulted in no alteration in the number, track length and movement speed of EB1-GFP comets in patronin RNAi dendrites (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Single RNAi knockdown of klp10A did not alter the direction of EB1-GFP movements in ddaC dendrites.
source: As a control, single RNAi knockdown of klp10A did not alter the direction of EB1-GFP movements in ddaC dendrites (n = 12; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of klp10A almost completely restored dendritic distribution of Nod-β-gal in patronin RNAi #1 ddaC neurons.
source: However, knockdown of klp10A (RNAi #1) almost completely restored dendritic distribution of Nod-β-gal in patronin RNAi #1 ddaC neurons (I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I and quantified in Figure 6J and K.

claim: Mis-localization of the axonal marker Kin-β-gal to the dendrites in patronin RNAi neurons was rescued by further knockdown of klp10A.
source: Likewise, mis-localization of the axonal marker Kin-β-gal to the dendrites in patronin RNAi neurons was rescued by further knockdown of klp10A (22%, n = 18, Figure 6N and O), compared to the control RNAi construct (85%, n = 20, Figure 6M and O).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6N and quantified in Figure 6O.

claim: The pruning defects associated with patronin RNAi ddaC neurons were almost completely rescued by further knockdown of klp10A.
source: Importantly, the pruning defects associated with patronin RNAi ddaC neurons were almost completely rescued by further knockdown of klp10A (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and C and quantified in Figure 7D and E.

claim: On average, only 73 µm and 71 µm of dendrites were present at 16 hr APF in patronin +klp10A #1 or #2 double RNAi ddaC neurons.
source: On average, only 73 µm and 71 µm of dendrites were present at 16 hr APF in patronin +klp10A #1 or #2 double RNAi ddaC neurons (n = 20, Figure 7B and D and n = 32, Figure 7C and D, respectively).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 7D.

claim: The penetrance of severing defects in patronin +klp10A #1 or patronin +klp10A #2 double RNAi ddaC neurons was drastically reduced to 15% and 19%, respectively.
source: Moreover, the penetrance of severing defects in patronin +klp10A #1 or patronin +klp10A #2 double RNAi ddaC neurons (Figure 7E) was drastically reduced to 15% and 19%, respectively, in contrast to 84% in the patronin +control RNAi controls (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 7E.

claim: Knockdown of either klp10A RNAi #1 or #2 did not cause any dendrite pruning defects in 16-h-APF ddaC neurons.
source: As controls, knockdown of either klp10A RNAi #1 or #2 did not cause any dendrite pruning defects in 16-h-APF ddaC neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of klp10A significantly suppressed the dendrite pruning defects in Patronin-overexpressing ddaC neurons.
source: Knockdown of klp10A, via two independent RNAi lines, significantly suppressed the dendrite pruning defects in Patronin-overexpressing ddaC neurons (n = 17 and 24; Figure 7G–J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7G and H and quantified in Figure 7I and J.

claim: Knockdown of klp10A significantly suppressed the MT orientation defect in the dendrites of Patronin-overexpressing ddaC neurons.
source: Moreover, knockdown of klp10A also significantly suppressed the MT orientation defect in the dendrites of Patronin-overexpressing ddaC neurons (n = 14; Figure 7L–N), compared to the control neurons (n = 13, Figure 7K and M–N).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7L and quantified in Figure 7M and N.

claim: Overexpression of either GFP-Klp10A or Klp10A resulted in consistent severing pruning defects in 88% and 94% of neurons with the persistence of 662 µm and 722 µm dendrites present at 16 hr APF, respectively.
source: Overexpression of either GFP-Klp10A (n = 16, Figure 8B, D and E) or Klp10A (n = 16, Figure 8C, D and E) resulted in consistent severing pruning defects in 88% and 94% of neurons with the persistence of 662 µm and 722 µm dendrites present at 16 hr APF, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B and C and quantified in Figure 8D and E.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-Klp10A or Klp10A resulted in simplified dendrite arbors at WP stage.
source: Similar to patronin mutants, overexpression of GFP-Klp10A (n = 8; Figure 8B) or Klp10A (n = 8; Figure 8C) also resulted in simplified dendrite arbors at WP stage, suggesting that elevated Klp10A impairs initial dendrite arborization during growth.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: Overexpression of Klp10A resulted in reduced levels of Nod-β-gal in the dendrites.
source: Moreover, overexpression of Klp10A also resulted in reduced levels of Nod-β-gal in the dendrites (n = 17; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) and mis-localization of Kin-β-gal to the dendrites (n = 20; Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of Klp10A resulted in mis-localization of Kin-β-gal to the dendrites.
source: Moreover, overexpression of Klp10A also resulted in reduced levels of Nod-β-gal in the dendrites (n = 17; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) and mis-localization of Kin-β-gal to the dendrites (n = 20; Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Klp10A overexpression significantly increased the percentage of anterograde EB1-GFP movement in the dendrites (11%).
source: Consistently, Klp10A overexpression also significantly increased the percentage of anterograde EB1-GFP movement in the dendrites (11%, n = 16; Figure 8G–H), suggesting a dendritic MT orientation defect.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8G and quantified in Figure 8H.

claim: Klp10A overexpression did not cause a significant reduction in the number of EB1-GFP comets in the dendrites.
source: Klp10A overexpression did not caused a signification reduction in the number of EB1-GFP comets in the dendrites (Figure 8I), resembling the patronin RNAi knockdown.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 8I.

claim: Neither track length of EB1-GFP comets nor their speed was affected upon Klp10A overexpression.
source: In addition, neither track length of EB1-GFP comets nor their speed was affected upon Klp10A overexpression (Figure 8J–K).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 8J and K.

claim: The expression of the CKK domain alone significantly rescued the dendrite pruning defects in the patronin RNAi background at 16 hr APF.
source: To this end, we first confirmed that the expression of the CKK domain alone significantly rescued the dendrite pruning defects in the patronin RNAi background at 16 hr APF (n = 24; Figure 8—figure supplement 2A), similar to those in patroninc9-c5 ddaC neurons (Figure 3D, E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The expression of the CKK domain, rather than the CH domain, almost fully rescued Nod-β-gal distribution in the dendrites of patronin RNAi ddaC neurons.
source: Importantly, the expression of the CKK domain, rather than the CH domain, almost fully rescued Nod-β-gal distribution (n = 15; Figure 8—figure supplement 2B) as well as retrograde EB1-GFP comets in the dendrites of patronin RNAi ddaC neurons (n = 15; Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The expression of the CKK domain almost fully rescued retrograde EB1-GFP comets in the dendrites of patronin RNAi ddaC neurons.
source: Importantly, the expression of the CKK domain, rather than the CH domain, almost fully rescued Nod-β-gal distribution (n = 15; Figure 8—figure supplement 2B) as well as retrograde EB1-GFP comets in the dendrites of patronin RNAi ddaC neurons (n = 15; Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The expression of the CKK domain significantly suppressed the dendrite pruning defects in Klp10A-overexpressing ddaC neurons.
source: Moreover, the expression of the CKK domain significantly suppressed the dendrite pruning defects in Klp10A-overexpressing ddaC neurons (n = 30; Figure 8—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that the CKK domain is able to antagonize Klp10A's function during dendrite pruning.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The CKK domain is able to antagonize Klp10A's function during dendrite pruning.
source: Moreover, the expression of the CKK domain significantly suppressed the dendrite pruning defects in Klp10A-overexpressing ddaC neurons (n = 30; Figure 8—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that the CKK domain is able to antagonize Klp10A's function during dendrite pruning.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of Klp10A overexpression phenotype by CKK domain expression.

claim: cnnhk1 mutant ddaC neurons exhibited dendrite severing defects (52%).
source: We observed dendrite severing defects in cnnhk1 mutant ddaC neurons (52%, n = 23; Figure 8—figure supplement 3A) as well as APC1Q8, APC2N175K double mutant ddaC clones (60%, n = 10; Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A.

claim: APC1Q8, APC2N175K double mutant ddaC clones exhibited dendrite severing defects (60%).
source: We observed dendrite severing defects in cnnhk1 mutant ddaC neurons (52%, n = 23; Figure 8—figure supplement 3A) as well as APC1Q8, APC2N175K double mutant ddaC clones (60%, n = 10; Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3B.

claim: No dendrite pruning defect was observed in fustchN94 or tau RNAi ddaC neurons.
source: As controls, MT-associated proteins, Futsch and Tau, which regulate MT stability (Hummel et al., 2000; Herzmann et al., 2017), appear to be dispensable for dendrite pruning, as no dendrite pruning defect was observed in fustchN94 or tau RNAi ddaC neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C-D.

claim: Futsch and Tau appear to be dispensable for dendrite pruning.
source: As controls, MT-associated proteins, Futsch and Tau, which regulate MT stability (Hummel et al., 2000; Herzmann et al., 2017), appear to be dispensable for dendrite pruning, as no dendrite pruning defect was observed in fustchN94 or tau RNAi ddaC neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of pruning defects in futsch and tau mutants.
